passage: My name is Farida, and I remember the exact tone of Rafiq's voice at the gate. "Everyone is skipping the last two periods. You coming or what?" Five of them stood in a half-circle, Rafiq in the middle, the rest nodding. Nasreen looked at her shoes. Nobody said what would happen if I refused, but Rafiq added, "We'll just tell you about it after." That was the threat. My chest tightened as if I would lose the whole group, not just an afternoon. I said, "Not today, I have to submit my file." It was true, and a little less than the whole truth. They left. I sat in class with my heart thudding, and an hour later Nasreen sent one 👍.

qa.q: What did Rafiq add after asking whether Farida was coming?
qa.a: Rafiq added, "We'll just tell you about it after."

qa.q: Why did the sentence "We'll just tell you about it after" feel like a threat to Farida?
qa.a: It hinted at being left out, so Farida feared losing the whole group; the social cost felt bigger than the skipped classes and brought a tight, anxious feeling.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped, and what could Farida add next time?
qa.a: Farida gave a plain reason and stayed in class; next time Farida could also tell a trusted adult or Nasreen how pressured it felt.

qa.q: What might Nasreen have been feeling when looking at her shoes and later sending a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Nasreen may have shared the doubts but not dared to say no in front of the group; the thumbs-up later suggests quiet support for Farida.

grounding: A teenager is told that skipping class is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion, and the social threat feels bigger than the act.

passage: Coach's note, Tuesday practice. I noticed Karthik hanging back at the nets while Lokesh and three others whispered near the pavilion. Later Karthik told me Lokesh had said, "Everyone vapes, don't be the odd one out, or the trip group won't include you." Karthik was not sure what to do and was ashamed of seeming scared. I told him it was fair to say no and that telling me was not wrong. That evening I called his parents and the school counsellor, who will speak with the group about vaping this week. Karthik looked lighter when he left the ground. — Coach Malik

qa.q: What did Lokesh say would happen if Karthik did not join?
qa.a: Lokesh said the trip group would not include Karthik.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when telling the coach?
qa.a: Karthik felt unsure and ashamed of seeming scared; looking lighter afterwards shows relief at having told an adult.

qa.q: What turning point helped Karthik, and what was the sensible follow-up?
qa.a: Karthik telling Coach Malik was the turning point, and the coach responded the same evening by calling the parents and the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see the moment when Karthik hangs back from the group?
qa.a: Lokesh may feel the group needs everyone to join to feel united, so a refusal could feel like a threat to belonging rather than a judgement of the group.

grounding: A teenager is told that vaping is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion, and a coach helps by responding the same day.

passage:
So you asked about peer pressure. I'm Madhuri, Class 11, and honestly, it didn't feel like pressure at first. It felt like a question.
Sahil and the others were bunking last period to go to the lake. Sahil said, “Everyone does it, yaar. Even the toppers.” Then Kritika added, “If you don't come, don't bother saving us seats tomorrow.” She laughed, but nobody else did.
That second line is what stuck. The bunking itself was nothing. Losing the lunch table felt like losing half my life.
I went back to class. The next day they sat without me for two days. On the third, Kritika asked for my notes, and slowly things came back. It still scares me how big it felt.

qa.q: Where were Sahil and the others going?
qa.a: They were bunking last period to go to the lake.

qa.q: Why did Kritika's line stick with Madhuri so strongly?
qa.a: Madhuri felt scared of being shut out; losing the lunch table felt like losing half her life, much bigger than the bunking itself.

qa.q: What helped Madhuri, and what else might help someone in Madhuri's place?
qa.a: Staying calm and simply going back to class helped; finding one friend who also says no would make the lonely days easier.

qa.q: How might Kritika have seen her own threat?
qa.a: Kritika laughed as she said it, so she may have thought it was a joke, not realising it felt like a real threat.

grounding: A teenager describes being told everyone bunks, with a hint of exclusion, and how the social threat felt bigger than the act.

passage:
Monday: At the bus stop Joseph passed round a vape. “Everyone does it, Irfan. Take one.” Irfan shook his head. Dev said, “Suit yourself,” and they all turned slightly away. On the ride home Irfan felt like a stranger among them.
Friday: The same offer, and this time Joseph added, “Maybe you'd like the front seats better.” Irfan's hands were cold. He almost reached out. Then he said, “Nah, my throat's bad,” and looked at his phone until the bus came.
The next Wednesday: Dev sat beside him and asked about the match. Joseph didn't speak to him all week. Irfan noticed that the bus ride was still just a bus ride.

qa.q: What excuse did Irfan give on Friday?
qa.a: He said, "Nah, my throat's bad."

qa.q: What does Irfan's cold hands on Friday suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt frightened and pressured; the hint of being pushed out made him almost reach for the vape even though he didn't want it.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan keep saying no?
qa.a: He could spend more time with Dev, who still talks to him, so the threat of being left out has less power.

qa.q: How does Dev seem to feel about Irfan's refusal by Wednesday?
qa.a: Dev seems relaxed about it; he chooses to sit with Irfan and talk about the match, showing not everyone cares as much as Joseph.

grounding: Shows a teenager told everyone vapes with a hint of exclusion, where the social threat feels bigger than the act itself.

passage:
Zubin, you're fifteen now, so listen to something from your Manjula aunty's school days.
The new maths teacher, Mr D'Souza, was very shy. My whole gang decided to hide the duster and chalk before his class. Leela said, “Everybody's doing it, Manju. If you back out, you're not one of us.”
I felt sick all morning. Not about the chalk, you know, but about being alone at lunch.
When the bell went, I stood at the door and couldn't make myself go in first. Then I watched him search the table, go pink, and apologise to us, of all things. That's when I went to the cupboard and handed him the chalk. Leela didn't speak to me for a week. Mr D'Souza thanked me every day for a month.

qa.q: What did the gang decide to hide before class?
qa.a: They decided to hide the duster and chalk.

qa.q: What was young Manjula most afraid of that morning?
qa.a: She was afraid of being alone at lunch; she felt sick about losing her gang, not about the prank itself.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Manjula's choice?
qa.a: Watching Mr D'Souza go pink and apologise made her see the real cost, so she handed him the chalk despite Leela's threat.

qa.q: How might Mr D'Souza have experienced that class?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and flustered, then grateful, which is why he thanked Manjula every day for a month.

grounding: An elder recalls being told a prank is what everyone does, with a threat of exclusion that felt bigger than the prank itself.

passage: It was the last period before the exam holidays, the fans in Class 10C had stopped working, and the room was an oven. Vaibhav leaned over. 'Everyone's bunking maths and going to the chaat corner. Coming?' Urmila looked around. Half the back row was packing up. 'Everyone?' 'Everyone who matters,' Vaibhav said, grinning. 'Unless you want to sit here with the nerds.' Her face went hot. Missing one class didn't seem like much. Being left out of the group photo later felt enormous. She thought of the revision the teacher had promised to go through today. Her hand hovered over her bag. Then Nisha, from the front row, turned round. 'I'm staying. Sit with me?' Urmila let out a breath and stayed. Vaibhav rolled his eyes.

qa.q: Where were the students going if they bunked maths?
qa.a: To the chaat corner.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's face go hot?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious at the hint that staying would leave her out with 'the nerds'.

qa.q: What helped Urmila resist the pressure?
qa.a: Nisha's invitation to sit together, one ally, and remembering the revision promised for that day.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel when Urmila stays?
qa.a: Irritated or let down, rolling his eyes because his 'everyone' claim didn't work.

grounding: A teenager on a hot, restless day is told everyone is bunking class, with a hint of exclusion, and the social threat feels bigger than the act.
